Base metal prices again performed strongly in February with the Thomson Reuters GFMS Base Metals Index, which gives equal weight to all of the base metals, rising to an average of 313, up from 296 in January.  In the absence of major fundamental news the markets have been driven more by macro and financial factors.  The focus has tended to be on the more upbeat numbers emanating from the United States rather than data relating to the Eurozone.  (See economic indicators for details).  However, confirmation that the Chinese government has lowered its growth target to 7.5% for 2012 triggered a correction in early March. 

The supply position for lead differs slightly from that of its “sister” metal, zinc.  The International Lead Zinc Study Group (ILZSG) estimates that refined lead increased by 7.2% in 2011.  A 9.8% increase to mine output allowed primary output to rise by 10.9%, while secondary output registered a 4.2% gain.  For zinc, there was a strong growth in mine production of 6.2%; however the increase to primary refined output was just under 2%.  This reflected largely unchanged output in China, following a number of years of exceptionally strong growth as smelters limited output for a mixture of financial and power-related reasons. 

The various statistical organisations have started to release their full year figures for 2011.  The production data highlights the very different supply sides for the individual metals. The International Copper Study Group (ICSG) figures (up to November) show a 0.1% increase to global mine supply.  Cochilco has published the official data on Chilean output last year.  They merely confirm the myriad of problems that saw output fall by 3.2% to 5.243m tonnes of copper in concentrate.  Data from the Peruvian Mines & Energy ministry show a 1% decline in concentrate output to 1.235m tonnes and a 5.5% fall in refined output to 227,000 tonnes.  The ICSG data suggest that the mine utilisation rate is set to fall for the seventh year in a row to below 79%. This compares with over 90% in 2004 and closer to 95% in 2001. 

Nickel and tin are also at the opposite end of the supply spectrum, with output rising sharply for the former, while structural tightness at the concentrate stage characterises the tin industry.  For nickel, although most of the attention is focused on the greenfield projects (a mixture of ferronickel and HPAL plants), output is already rising sharply. Thomson Reuters GFMS estimate that global refined nickel production increased by 8.9% last year.  Most of the increase reflected the recovery from earlier strike related losses at Vale’s Canadian operations and sharply higher nickel pig iron production in China.  This year the growth will more reflect the new capacity that is being developed.  For tin, there were only limited gains to mine production, which once again constrained th

e growth in refined tin production. According to the figures from the WBMS, global tin-in concentrate production in 2011 was 12.7% below that seen in 2007. There are few major projects in the pipeline that will alleviate the tightness in the short term. We note that output fell at three of the four largest producers of refined tin last year. This tightness at the raw material stage is in sharp contrast to the aluminium sector. The International Aluminium Institute (IAI) data confirm the significant gains in global alumina production with a 6.5% gain last year to 92.108m tonnes following an 11.6% increase in 2010. China has been the key driver behind the sharp increase to alumina supply in recent years. According to Antaike, the Beijingbased research organisation, the country’s alumina capacity at the end of last year stood at 51.42m tonnes, up 10.5m on the end 2010 figure. Vehicle sales surged to a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 15.1m units in February up from 14.1m units in January and is the highest level for nearly 4 years. Although the index improved marginally in February to 94.4, from 93.4 in January, all of the sub indices – industrial, construction, consumer and retail trade – remain in negative territory. The Commission expects the region’s economic output to contract by 0.3% this year. Unemployment continues to weigh heavily on consumer sentiment. The rate has risen for the last seven months, touching 10.7% in February, up from the 10% level that characterised the first half of last year. This figure, of course, masks huge differences within the region with the rate in excess of 23% in Spain and moving close to 5% in Germany. The results of the various purchasing managers’ surveys outside of the US are less positive for the base metal producers. Conflicting signals are coming from China. The official PMI rose to 51.0 in February up from 50.5 in January with the survey citing an increase in the new export orders sub index to 51.1, the highest reading since May 2011. The HSBC PMI highlights a poor export performance (its sub index slid to an eight month low of 47.5). Overall the HSBC index remained under 50 for the fifth month in a row. The latest GDP numbers confirm the slowdown in the rate of expansion underway in India. GDP registered growth of 6.1% in Q4. And this represented the sixth decline in the last seven quarters. In early 2010, growth was running at close to 10%. Activity continues to be affected by poor business confidence and the high interest rate environment as the government tries to curb the inflationary pressures. In this respect the Indian government has been successful with the whole price index in January at 6.6%, down from over 9.5% in the final quarter of last year. The European PMI published by Markit Economics is also under 50, while the European Commissions’ economic sentiment index is below the long-term average of 100. Although there is no doubt that the inventory accumulation for alu

minium has been much greater than for the other base metals, the situation has been clouded by the intertwined issues of financing deals, low interest rates, competitive warehousing deals (and the ownership of warehouses) as well as load out rates. One result of recent changes is that cancelled warrants no longer provide such a key indicator of future movements in LME inventories as increasingly they can merely reflect movements from one warehouse to another. Many of the factors that have encouraged financing deals – low interest rates, competitive warehousing costs and a contango market – remain in place; however, from a fundamental standpoint the on-going rise in stocks, irrespective of whether they are available to the market, should limit the gains in the aluminium price. The data on exchange and producer inventories continue to highlight the ready availability of material. In addition, producer and Japanese port stocks have increased by around 200,000 tonnes and 50,000 tonnes respectively in recent months, while “unreported” stocks are also moving higher. Although Thomson Reuters GFMS’ supply-demand balance analysis suggest that the aluminium market will be a deficit for 2012, the forecast stock draw down of 130,000 tonnes will make little impact on the huge inventory overhang. ###### **Raw material tightness – is it an issue for the aluminium industry?** When assessing the underlying fundamentals, the individual base metals can be placed in two camps – those that are characterised by tightness at the raw material stage and those where raw material is readily available. For example, copper firmly resides the former camp, while aluminium is at the other extreme. The latest figures from the International Aluminium Institute (IAI) highlight the significant gains in global alumina production. They suggest a 6.5% rise last year to 92.108m tonnes, following an 11.6% increase in 2010. By comparison, global copper concentrate production increased by 0.8% and 0.2% in this period, which in turn has contributed only modest gains in copper cathode output. According to the IAI, primary aluminium production in 2010 increased by 10.7% and by 7.4% in 2011. China has been the key driver behind the sharp increase in alumina supply in recent years. For example, in 2005 the country accounted for 13% of total output with domestic production of 8.51 million tonnes. Since then, Chinese alumina production has expanded rapidly. In 2010, output rose by 21.7% which, followed by a 17.7% increase last year, took output to 34.078 million tonnes in 2011, accounting for 37% of global production.

Part of the decline reflects the temporary stoppages at Rio Tinto Alcan’s Canadian operations, where a labour dispute at its 438,000 tpy Alma plant has reduced output by two thirds and where a circuit failure saw output halved at its 100,000 tpy Shawinigan plant. However, the company has started to bring the potlines back online at Shawinigan and full capacity should be achieved during the second quarter. Alcoa has recently announced a review on the future of its 190,000 tpy Point Henry primary aluminium smelter in Australia, which is currently unprofitable due to higher input costs and adverse movements in the exchange rates. ###### **Alumina capacity continues to expand** Alumina production outside of China rose by just 0.9% last year to 58.030 million tonnes. Higher prices encouraged the restart of previously idled capacity at Gyandja in Azerbaijan and at Ormet in the United States towards the end of 2011; both plants have a capacity of around 500,000 tpy. Also there were brownfield expansions at ENRC (Kazakhstan), Nalco (India), Glencore (United States), and Vinacomin (Vietnam), which combined added just over 1.5million tonnes to capacity. However, the bulk of the production and capacity growth once again took place in China. According to Antaike, the Beijing-based research organisation, the country’s alumina capacity at the end of last year stood at 51.42 million tonnes, up 10.51 million tonnes on the end 2010 figure. According to the IAI, Chinese alumina output was 34.078 million tonnes last year implying a capacity utilisation rate of under 70%. Given the recent increase to aluminium prices and the ready availability of alumina we do not expect any significant declines in Chinese aluminium production. In last month’s issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, we noted both the surge in service center shipments in the United States (up 15% in 2011) and the upbeat projections on extrusion demand from Sapa (5-7% growth in 2012). This positive outlook has been reinforced by the latest durable good numbers. In February, the primary metal orders component rose by 5.6% year-on-year, while orders at metal fabricators were 4.2% higher. The US Midwest premium has increased sharply with some smaller deals commanding a premium of close to $200/ tonne. The low end of the range for billet premiums is now $265/tonne, up from $245/tonne, a level that had been in place since last summer. The rise in premiums reflects both production outages and more importantly an improvement in demand. The demand situation in China is still clouded by the Lunar New Year holidays in that all indicators show sharp year-onyear and month-on-month declines in January. However, the anecdotal evidence that we receive suggest that consumption has been slow to pick up after the holiday period. The market is not helped by the government’s move to cool certain parts of the real estate market as well as by the recent downgrading of economic growth targets. ###### **Market outlook** It would appear that the aluminium market is beginning to live with the high level of inventories.
